walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations of Physics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations of Physics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations of Physics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
options: Energy
Force
Mass
Temperature

mcqs.q: Expressed in SI base units, the newton is:
options: kg m s⁻¹
kg s⁻²
kg m s⁻²
kg m² s⁻²
Velocity
Momentum
Energy
Displacement

mcqs.q: Forces of 3 N and 4 N act on an object at right angles. The magnitude of the resultant is:
options: 1 N
5 N
7 N

mcqs.q: Is speed the same thing as velocity?
options: No — forces can never partially cancel.
No — speed is a scalar; velocity includes direction, so equal speeds can be different velocities.
No — velocity is always larger than speed.
Yes — they are interchangeable words for how fast something moves.

mcqs.q: Can forces of 3 N and 4 N combine to give a resultant of 1 N?
options: Yes — but only for distances.
No — 3 N plus 4 N always makes 7 N.
Yes — if they act in opposite directions; a vector sum depends on direction.
No — forces can never partially cancel.

mcqs.q: Once you have the number, does the unit still matter?
options: Yes — but only for distances.
Yes — a value is meaningless without its unit, and units must stay consistent through equations.
No — velocity is always larger than speed.
No — the number alone is the answer.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “SI base units”?
options: The metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole underpin all derived units in physics.
A measurable quantity consisting of a numerical magnitude together with a unit.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically F cos θ and F sin θ.
Units built from base units; for example, the newton is kg m s⁻².

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Resolving a vector”?
options: Units built from base units; for example, the newton is kg m s⁻².
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity or force.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically F cos θ and F sin θ.
The metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole underpin all derived units in physics.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Derived units”?
options: A measurable quantity consisting of a numerical magnitude together with a unit.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity or force.
Units built from base units; for example, the newton is kg m s⁻².
The metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole underpin all derived units in physics.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Scalar”?
options: A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity or force.
The metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole underpin all derived units in physics.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, energy, speed or temperature.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically F cos θ and F sin θ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Physical quantity”?
options: A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, energy, speed or temperature.
Units built from base units; for example, the newton is kg m s⁻².
The metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole underpin all derived units in physics.
A measurable quantity consisting of a numerical magnitude together with a unit.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vector”?
options: Units built from base units; for example, the newton is kg m s⁻².
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity or force.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically F cos θ and F sin θ.
The metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole underpin all derived units in physics.

options: 5 N
